The difference that matters

A walkaround is
inventory. An ad is an argument.

Most vehicle video is documentation — proof the car exists, shot the same way for every unit on the lot. Useful. Not persuasive. We make both, and we do not pretend they are the same thing.

Walkaround

Every VIN

One template, run across the whole lot. Exterior orbit, interior, dash, wheels. Twenty seconds. It goes on the vehicle detail page and it makes a static gallery feel alive.

It is identical for every unit — and that is the point. A dealer with 300 cars cannot brief 300 films.

Priced as a commodity, sold by the month.

Ad cut

One vehicle

Briefed to the unit. A Ferrari opens on the badge and snaps between beats at hype tempo. A Silverado opens wide on the stance, holds on the bed and the red leather, and moves with weight.

Same anchoring engine, different argument. Tempo, opening frame, closing frame, which details get a push and which get skipped — all of it changes per vehicle.

Priced against the marketing budget the unit already carries.

The second one is what we actually sell. The first one is how we get in the door.

The part nobody else ships

Disclosure,
already handled.

An AI video that looks like drone footage is a disclosure problem even when every source photo is genuine. The images are real. The flight is not.

What the rules actually say

NAR Code of Ethics, Article 12 requires REALTORS® to present a true picture and to disclose the status of any altered photograph. It binds every REALTOR®, in every state.

California AB 723 — Business & Professions Code §10140.8, effective 1 January 2026 — requires a conspicuous statement that an image was modified and a link to the original unaltered image by URL or QR code. It reaches "a person acting on their behalf", which means your vendor too.

MLS penalties for non-disclosure commonly run $500–$5,000.

Most AI video ships you a file and a liability. Every delivery of ours arrives with the disclosure card burned into the video, a QR code, ready-to-paste MLS remark text, and a hosted page carrying your unaltered originals — which is the artefact the statute actually asks for.

We never retouch, stage or colour-correct what you send. Not a limitation — the moment we edit a photo, that originals page stops containing originals, and the position collapses for both of us.

Not legal advice. Rules vary by MLS and state. Have your broker's counsel review the disclosure text.
